otherNames.name: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
otherNames.note: the fullest form in the book titles of some copies of the Divine Institutes

knownFor: A teacher of Latin public speaking from Africa, Jerome says, who was teaching at Nicomedia in Bithynia when the Great Persecution began in 303. He answered it with the Divine Institutes, seven books arguing the faith to educated pagans from their own philosophers and historians, which hold that religion cannot be forced. In extreme old age, Jerome says, he taught Constantine's son Crispus in Gaul.
shortDescription: Lactantius was teaching Latin public speaking at Nicomedia, the city where the emperor Diocletian kept his palace, when the Great Persecution began in 303. He answered it with the Divine Institutes, seven books that argue the faith to educated pagans and hold that religion cannot be forced.
datesNote: No old source gives the year of his birth or of his death. He was teaching in Bithynia when the persecution began, in the nineteenth year of the emperor Diocletian as Eusebius counts it, so in 303. His own books were written during and after the persecution, which they describe, and name no year. Jerome puts his teaching of Crispus in his extreme old age.
placeNote: From Africa, Jerome says, who tells of a verse account of his journey from Africa to Nicomedia. Nicomedia was a Greek-speaking city in Bithynia, a Roman province on the Black Sea in north-west Asia Minor, now north-west Turkey. The emperor Diocletian had his palace there, and Lactantius taught Latin public speaking there. Later Gaul, where Jerome says he taught Crispus; Jerome names no city.
role: Teacher of Latin public speaking at Nicomedia; Christian writer in Latin

keyWorks.title: Divine Institutes
keyWorks.about: seven books arguing the faith to educated pagans from their own philosophers and historians. He took the title from the lawyers' handbooks of the civil law, called Institutes, written to settle quarrels; his are on hope, life, salvation, immortality and God. Book I argues that the pagan gods had once been men, and calls the Sibyls, prophetesses whose verses the pagans kept, as witnesses against them. Book II traces the origin of error, and Book III sets the philosophers against one another. Book IV joins true wisdom and religion, holding that there is no religion without wisdom, nor wisdom without religion. Book V turns to the persecution and holds that religion cannot be forced, and must be defended by dying, not by killing. Book VI is on true worship. Book VII holds that the world lasts six thousand years, and that righteousness then reigns on earth for a thousand. Some copies open with an address to the emperor Constantine, and whether Lactantius wrote it is disputed

keyWorks.title: On the Workmanship of God
keyWorks.about: a short book on the making of man, addressed to Demetrianus, which Jerome calls On the work of God or the creation of man. It opens with Lactantius writing that he is disturbed, and in the greatest necessities

keyWorks.title: On the Deaths of the Persecutors
keyWorks.about: a book of disputed authorship, which survives in one copy under the name Lucius Caecilius. It is addressed to Donatus, who had been tortured nine times and was freed from a jail where he had lain six years. It tells how the emperors who persecuted the Christians died, so that later generations might learn from it. It tells of the fall of the church at Nicomedia, the edicts, and Galerius's disease and his edict letting Christians be Christians again. It tells of Constantine's dream before battle, the edict of Milan posted at Nicomedia, and the killing of the persecutors' families, among them a boy of eight and a girl of seven. It counts ten years and about four months from the overthrow of the church to its restoration. The Library holds it in English, in Lord Hailes' translation, and its chapter 48, the edict of Milan, in Latin

traces: Lucifer of Cagliari, a bishop, wrote to the emperor Constantius, Constantine's son, who backed the Arian teaching that there was a time when the Son of God did not exist. He took over Lactantius's sentences on defending religion by dying, not by killing, without naming him, and turned them on the emperor.
Augustine says Lactantius brought in the Sibylline testimonies bit by bit as his argument needed them, and that he himself set them down in one connected series in the City of God.
In On Christian Teaching, Augustine counts Lactantius among the faithful who came out of Egypt loaded with its gold, his image for pagan learning taken into Christian use.

The book on the persecutors' deaths keeps the text of two imperial orders: Galerius's edict letting Christians be Christians again, and the edict of Milan, which gave Christians and all others the freedom to follow the religion each chose, and whose Latin survives there.
Calvin ends one argument with Lactantius, that no religion is genuine that is not in accordance with truth, and tells readers to read Lactantius and Eusebius on images.

In a letter to the parish priest of Cernex, Calvin calls Lactantius an ancient doctor of the Church, meaning one of its early teachers. He writes that Lactantius and Augustine show that in their time the world's troubles were blamed on the Gospel, because it had done away with the pagan rites.
remembered: Jerome says Lactantius has a flow of eloquence worthy of Tully, meaning Cicero, and wishes he could have built up the faith as easily as he tore down that of others.
Jerome writes that in Lactantius's books one finds a summary of Cicero's dialogues.

Jerome charges that Lactantius, in his books and above all in his letters to Demetrian, denies the Holy Spirit a being of his own. He takes the passages on the Spirit, Jerome says, to mean the Father or the Son. Yet Jerome asks who can forbid him to read the Institutes, in which Lactantius wrote against the pagans with much ability.
Jerome's Chronicle calls him the most eloquent man of his time and says he was so poor in this life that he often lacked even the necessities.
Jerome counts him among those who held that after the resurrection the Lord would reign in the flesh with the saints.
A list of books received and not received, which its heading credits to Pope Gelasius and a second copy to Pope Hormisdas, sets the little works of Lactantius among the books not received.

uncertain: Most of his life outside his own books rests on one witness, Jerome, who wrote later in the same century. Lactantius himself says only that he was called to Bithynia to teach, and names no one who called him.
Where he was born. Jerome says he came from Africa, and no old source names the place of his birth.

Where he wrote his Banquet. The English of Jerome's notice and one Latin print say he wrote it as a young man in Africa; the other Latin print lacks the words in Africa. Both have the journey from Africa to Nicomedia.

His name. Jerome calls him Firmianus, known also as Lactantius. Some copies of the Divine Institutes call him Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius in their book titles, some with the first name Lucius. The one copy of the book on the persecutors' deaths names its author Lucius Caecilius.
When and where he became a Christian is not known. He was one when the persecution began, since he writes that the attacks on the Christians were published in his presence and to his grief.

Whether he saw the church fall. He writes only that he was teaching in Bithynia when the temple of God was overthrown, and does not say he watched it. The scene of the church at Nicomedia leveled is told in the book on the persecutors' deaths.

Who wrote the book on the persecutors' deaths is disputed. It survives in one copy, which names its author Lucius Caecilius. Jerome lists among Lactantius's books one On persecution, and no old source says it is this book.

The cause of the palace fire at Nicomedia. The book on the persecutors' deaths says Galerius's agents set it, and the blame was laid on the Christians. Eusebius says it broke out he knows not how, and was laid on the Christians through a false suspicion. Constantine, in the speech Eusebius keeps, says lightning destroyed the palace and the emperor's chamber, and that eyewitnesses, he among them, declare it.
The address to Constantine. Some copies of the Divine Institutes open with an address to the emperor Constantine, and others lack it. Whether Lactantius wrote it is disputed.
The two writers he answers. The philosopher who praised poverty and the judge who pressed for the persecution are not named in the Divine Institutes.
When he taught Crispus. Jerome puts it in his extreme old age, and gives no year.
How, when and where he died is not known.

briefReferences: Divine Institutes V.11, tr. William Fletcher, and Brandt's Latin: the governor in Bithynia elated because one man who had held out for two years seemed at last to give way; governors who boasted that they had shed no blood; judges who knew it was a contest and tortured to win.

Divine Institutes V.2: he was teaching in Bithynia, having been called there, when the temple of God was overthrown. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80: from Africa, and called to Nicomedia. Eusebius, Church History VIII.2 and VIII.6: the first edict, in the nineteenth year of Diocletian, and the palace at Nicomedia.
Divine Institutes V.20 (Brandt's V.19): the persecutors seek to make Christians worship the gods by force and tortures.

Divine Institutes V.2 to V.4: the two men who published books against the Christians in his presence and to his grief, the philosopher who praised poverty and the judge who pressed for the persecution.

Divine Institutes V.1 and V.4: Tertullian learned in literature of every kind but very obscure; Cyprian the most renowned, who answered Demetrianus with Scripture the man thought false; the beginner fed milk and refuted by his own authorities.

Divine Institutes I.1, I.15, II and III: the title taken from the lawyers' Institutes of the civil law; the gods who had once been men; the philosophers who refute one another; no religion without wisdom, nor wisdom without religion.

Divine Institutes V.20 (Brandt's V.19): religion cannot be compelled and must be carried on by words rather than blows; the pagans say their rites must be defended; religion is to be defended by dying, not by killing.

On the Deaths of the Persecutors, a book of disputed authorship in one copy under the name Lucius Caecilius; chapter 44: the dream that directed Constantine to mark his soldiers' shields with the sign of Christ.
Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80: in extreme old age, tutor to Constantine's son Crispus in Gaul.

Jerome, Letter 58, in English and Latin: the wish that Lactantius could have built up the faith as easily as he tore down that of others. Jerome, Letter 84: who can forbid him to read the Institutes, written against the pagans with much ability.

Lucifer of Cagliari, We must die for the Son of God, to the emperor Constantius: the Arian teaching defended with the sword, and religion defended by dying for God, in Lactantius's own sentences recast; Divine Institutes V.19 in Brandt's Latin. Socrates, Church History I.5: Arius's teaching that there was a time when the Son was not.
Jerome, Chronicle: the most eloquent man of his time, yet so poor in this life that he often lacked even what he needed.

quotationOriginals.modern: I myself saw in Bithynia a governor astonishingly elated with joy, as if he had conquered some nation of barbarians. It was because one man, who had held out for two years with great courage, seemed at last to give way.
quotationOriginals.printed: uidi ego in Bithynia praesidem gaudio mirabiliter elatum tamquam barbarorum gentem aliquam subegisset, quod unus qui per biennium magna uirtute restiterat, postremo cedere uisus esset
quotationOriginals.work: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.11.15, Latin ed. Samuel Brandt, English tr. William Fletcher
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: I saw in Bithynia the præfect wonderfully elated with joy, as though he had subdued some nation of barbarians, because one who had resisted for two years with great spirit appeared at length to yield
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Brandt's Latin, not Fletcher's English. Uidi ego is I myself saw. Fletcher's præfect is the brief's governor (praesidem, the governor of a province), and his wonderfully is the brief's astonishingly (mirabiliter). It was because renders quod. A second scan of Brandt's edition reads the same Latin (lines 33611-33614 of that file).

quotationOriginals.work: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.2.2, Latin ed. Samuel Brandt, English tr. William Fletcher
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: the temple of God was overthrown
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Brandt's Latin, which agrees with Fletcher's English word for word. Lactantius does not say whether he means the church building at Nicomedia or the church at large.

quotationOriginals.work: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.19.6 (chapter 20 in the English edition), Latin ed. Samuel Brandt, English tr. William Fletcher

quotationOriginals.work: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.4.1, Latin ed. Samuel Brandt, English tr. William Fletcher

quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Brandt's Latin, which agrees with Fletcher's English word for word.

quotationOriginals.modern: For religion must be defended not by killing but by dying, not by cruelty but by endurance, not by crime but by faithfulness.
quotationOriginals.printed: defendenda enim religio est non occidendo sed moriendo, non saeuitia sed patientia, non scelere sed fide
quotationOriginals.work: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.19.22 (chapter 20 in the English edition), Latin ed. Samuel Brandt, English tr. William Fletcher
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: For religion is to be defended, not by putting to death, but by dying; not by cruelty, but by patient endurance; not by guilt, but by good faith
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Brandt's Latin, not Fletcher's English. Fletcher's putting to death is the brief's killing (occidendo). Patientia is endurance under suffering. Fides here is keeping faith, as a soldier keeps faith with his king in the lines that follow, so the brief has faithfulness for Fletcher's good faith, and crime for his guilt (scelere). A second scan of Brandt's edition reads the same Latin.

timeline.headline: From Africa to a Greek city in Bithynia
timeline.witness: Jerome, writing later in the same century, unless a line says otherwise

lines.text: Jerome calls him Firmianus, known also as Lactantius, a pupil of Arnobius, who taught rhetoric, the art of public speaking, at Sicca in Africa.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 79 and 80, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41022-41034

lines.text: As a young man he writes a Banquet, and later an Itinerary, a journey from Africa to Nicomedia told in verse.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41038-41041; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_de-opificio-de-ira-carmina-lat_brandt-csel27-1.txt lines 11186-11187
lines.note: The two Latin prints of Jerome differ on whether the Banquet was written in Africa.

lines.text: He is summoned to Nicomedia, with Flavius the Grammarian, and teaches rhetoric there.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41035-41037

lines.text: He writes that he was called to Bithynia to teach public speaking, and names no one who called him.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.2, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4487; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt line 22774

lines.text: Pupils are few, since it is a Greek city, so he turns to writing.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41036-41038

lines.text: He says he gained some skill in speaking for the sake of teaching, but was never eloquent himself, since he never so much as set foot in the forum, where cases were pleaded.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes III.13, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 2487; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 12295-12296

timeline.headline: The Great Persecution begins while he teaches in Bithynia

lines.text: Imperial edicts order the churches leveled and the Scriptures burned, Christians who hold places of honor degraded, and Christian household servants who keep the faith deprived of freedom.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VIII.2.4, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 43460-43491
lines.note: Eusebius, who lived through the persecution.

lines.text: Lactantius is teaching in Bithynia when, as he puts it, the temple of God is overthrown.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.2, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4487; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 22774-22775
lines.note: He does not say he watched it.

lines.text: The book on the persecutors' deaths tells how the church at Nicomedia, within view of the palace, is forced open at first light. Its Scriptures are burned, and the Pretorian Guards level it in a few hours.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 12, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10161

lines.text: The next day an edict strips Christians of all honors and dignities and makes them subject to torture whatever their rank. A man who tears it down is tortured and burned alive.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 13, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10174; Eusebius, Church History VIII.5, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 43835-43838
lines.note: A book of disputed authorship; Eusebius also tells of the man who tore down the edict.

lines.text: Fire breaks out in the palace at Nicomedia, and the blame is laid on the Christians.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 14, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10185; Eusebius, Church History VIII.6, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 43982-43984; Constantine, Oration to the Assembly of the Saints 25, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 70323-70325
lines.note: The three old accounts differ on its cause: Galerius's agents, a cause Eusebius says he does not know, or lightning.

lines.text: Presbyters and other officers of the church are led to execution with their families, people are burned in crowds, and servants are thrown into the sea with millstones tied about their necks.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 15, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10198

lines.text: Lactantius writes that the persecutors seek to make Christians worship the gods by force and tortures.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.20, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 5136; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt line 26072

lines.text: He tells of governors who boasted that they had shed no blood, and of judges who tortured slowly to win, since they knew it was a contest and a battle.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.11, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4899; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 24570-24574

lines.text: He writes that he saw a governor in Bithynia full of joy because one man, who had held out for two years, seemed at last to give way.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.11, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4899; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 24576-24579
lines.note: He says he saw this himself.

lines.text: He writes of a man in Phrygia who burned a whole congregation together with their meeting place.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.11, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4897
lines.note: He does not say he saw it.

lines.text: A philosopher who praised poverty, yet dined less richly in a palace than at his own house, publishes three books saying a philosopher's duty is to call people back to the worship of the gods.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.2, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 4487-4497
lines.note: Lactantius's portrait of him; he gives no name.

lines.text: A judge who had pressed for the persecution writes two books to the Christians, as if out of kindness, to prove that their Scripture contradicts itself.
lines.reference: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.2, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4505
lines.note: Lactantius's portrait of him; he gives no name.

timeline.when: Date unknown; during and after the persecution
timeline.headline: The Divine Institutes, an answer to the persecution

lines.text: He takes up the task of answering the two men and all like them.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes V.4, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4567; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 23206-23210

lines.text: He writes that the learned scorn Scripture because the prophets spoke in plain, simple language, so wisdom and truth need skilled speakers to defend them.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes V.1, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 4460, 4468

lines.text: Of the Christian writers before him, he finds Tertullian learned in literature of every kind but rough and very obscure, and Cyprian the most renowned.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes V.1, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 4472-4474

lines.text: He faults Cyprian for answering Demetrianus, a pagan, with Scripture the man thought false, instead of with argument and reason.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes V.4, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4573

lines.text: A newcomer, he writes, is like an infant who needs milk before solid food, and must be refuted by his own authorities, the philosophers and historians.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes V.4, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 4581

lines.text: He sets out to lead the learned to true wisdom and the unlearned to true religion. He calls this a better calling than the teaching of public speaking, in which, he writes, he trained young men not in virtue but in cunning wickedness.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes I.1, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 556; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 191-209

lines.text: He takes his title from the Institutes of the civil law that lawyers wrote to settle quarrels; his own are on hope, life, salvation, immortality and God.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes I.1, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 569; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 262-265

lines.text: Book I argues that the pagan gods had once been men, and calls the Sibyls, prophetesses whose verses the pagans kept, as witnesses.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes I.6 and I.15, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 692, 700, 1007-1009

lines.text: He holds that the philosophers disagree and refute one another, and that there is no religion without wisdom, nor wisdom without religion.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes I.1 and III.4, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 575, 584, 2300

lines.text: Book V holds that religion cannot be compelled, and must be carried on by words rather than blows, so that it is willing.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes V.20, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 5140; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 26133-26135

lines.text: To the pagans who say their rites must be defended, he agrees that religion must be defended with all one's strength, but by dying, not by killing.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes V.20, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 5156-5158; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 26236-26242

lines.text: Book VII holds that the world lasts six ages, six thousand years, and that righteousness then reigns on earth for a thousand years.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes VII.14, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 6648-6650

lines.text: Some copies open with an address to the emperor Constantine, hailing him as the first Roman ruler to honor the one true God.
lines.reference: Divine Institutes I.1, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 571; Latin apparatus, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-lat_brandt1890-csel-tei.txt lines 286-289
lines.note: Only some copies have it, and whether Lactantius wrote it is disputed.

lines.text: In On the Workmanship of God, addressed to Demetrianus, he writes that he is disturbed, and in the greatest necessities.
lines.reference: On the Workmanship of God 1, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 9310; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_de-opificio-de-ira-carmina-lat_brandt-csel27-1.txt line 3608

timeline.headline: Toleration, as the book on the persecutors' deaths tells it
timeline.witness: On the Deaths of the Persecutors, a book of disputed authorship

lines.text: Galerius, struck by disease, issues an edict letting Christians be Christians again and rebuild their places of assembly. It is posted at Nicomedia.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 33 to 35, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 10462, 10486, 10501

lines.text: Donatus, to whom the book is addressed, is freed with other confessors from a jail where he had lain six years.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 35, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10505; and 16, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10223
lines.note: The book says he had been tortured nine times.

lines.text: Constantine is directed in a dream to mark his soldiers' shields with the sign of Christ before his battle at Rome.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 44, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10620

lines.when: 313, the third consulship of Licinius and Constantine
lines.text: The edict of Milan, which grants Christians and all others the freedom to follow the religion each chooses, is posted at Nicomedia.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 48, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 10680-10684; Latin, cic/texts/mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt lines 4790-4796

lines.text: The book counts ten years and about four months from the overthrow of the church to its restoration.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 48, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10690

lines.text: It tells of the killing of the persecutors' families, among them a boy of eight and a girl of seven, and says all the wicked received according to their deeds.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 50, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 10712

lines.text: It says it was written so that all who are far off and all who come later may learn, and that its author relies on well-informed persons.
lines.reference: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 1 and 52, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 9987, 10736

timeline.when: Date unknown; in his extreme old age
timeline.headline: Teacher of Constantine's son in Gaul
timeline.witness: Jerome, writing later in the same century

lines.text: In his extreme old age he is tutor in Gaul to Crispus Caesar, a son of Constantine, who was later put to death by his father.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41051-41054; Latin, cic/texts/lactantius_de-opificio-de-ira-carmina-lat_brandt-csel27-1.txt lines 11223-11226

lines.text: The Chronicle calls him the most eloquent man of his time, yet so poor in this life that he often lacked even the necessities.
lines.reference: Jerome, Chronicle, cic/texts/jerome_eusebii-chronici-canones-lat_fotheringham1923.txt lines 44984-44986; cic/texts/lactantius_de-opificio-de-ira-carmina-lat_brandt-csel27-1.txt lines 11241-11243

lines.text: Jerome lists his books. Besides the Banquet and the Itinerary, they are the Grammarian, On the Anger of God, and the seven books of the Divine Institutes with a summary of them. Then come two books To Asclepiades, one On persecution, letters to Probus, Severus and his pupil Demetrius, and On the work of God.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41038-41051

lines.text: Lucifer of Cagliari, a bishop sent into exile under the emperor Constantius for refusing to condemn the faith of the council of Nicaea, which Athanasius stood for, writes to the emperor.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 95, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41266-41271; Lucifer, We must die for the Son of God, cic/texts/lucifer-cagliari_opuscula-lat_hartel1886-csel14.txt lines 15818-15820

lines.text: Lucifer tells Constantius that he defends the Arian teaching with the sword, but that religion is defended not by killing but by dying for God, in Lactantius's own sentences, recast and unnamed.
lines.reference: Lucifer, We must die for the Son of God, cic/texts/lucifer-cagliari_opuscula-lat_hartel1886-csel14.txt lines 16934-16942; Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.19, cic/texts/lactantius_divinae-institutiones-epitome-csel19-second-scan-lat_brandt1890.txt lines 35546-35550
lines.note: The Arian teaching, after Arius: that there was a time when the Son was not (Socrates, Church History I.5, npnf202 line 2096).

lines.text: Jerome says Lactantius has a flow of eloquence worthy of Cicero, and wishes he could have built up the faith as easily as he tore down that of others.
lines.reference: Jerome, Letter 58, cic/texts/npnf206_jerome-principal-works.xml lines 14112-14114; Latin, cic/texts/jerome_epistulae-1-70-lat_hilberg-csel54-1910.txt lines 27050-27052

lines.text: Jerome writes that in Lactantius's books one finds a summary of Cicero's dialogues.
lines.reference: Jerome, Letter 70, cic/texts/npnf206_jerome-principal-works.xml lines 16719-16721

lines.text: Jerome charges that Lactantius denies the Holy Spirit a being of his own, yet asks who can forbid him to read the Institutes, written against the pagans with much ability.
lines.reference: Jerome, Letter 84, cic/texts/npnf206_jerome-principal-works.xml lines 19203-19212

lines.when: About 392, the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius
lines.text: Jerome counts him among those who held that after the resurrection the Lord would reign in the flesh with the saints.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 18, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 39882-39885
lines.note: Jerome dates his Lives by that year (lines 38784-38785).

lines.text: Augustine sets Lactantius's Sibylline testimonies in one connected series, where Lactantius had brought them in bit by bit.
lines.reference: Augustine, City of God XVIII.23, cic/texts/npnf102_augustine-city-of-god-christian-doctrine.xml lines 35552-35555

lines.text: Augustine counts Lactantius among the faithful who came out of Egypt loaded with its gold.
lines.reference: Augustine, On Christian Teaching II.40, cic/texts/npnf102_augustine-city-of-god-christian-doctrine.xml lines 51718-51722

lines.text: A list of books received and not received, credited in its heading to Pope Gelasius and in a second copy to Pope Hormisdas, sets the little works of Lactantius among those not received.
lines.reference: Ancient witnesses to Lactantius, cic/texts/lactantius_de-opificio-de-ira-carmina-lat_brandt-csel27-1.txt lines 11463-11486

lines.text: Calvin ends one argument with Lactantius, that no religion is genuine that is not in accordance with truth, and tells readers to read Lactantius and Eusebius on images.
lines.reference: Calvin, Institutes I, cic/texts/calvin_institutes-christian-religion-vol1_beveridge1845.txt lines 7254-7256, 10123
